entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
ʿAmr ibn al-Jamūḥ was an ansari companion of Muhammad, and a chief of Banu Salama. He played a pivotal role in the early days of Islam, serving as a key leader in the Arabian Peninsula. Born into a prominent family, Amr ibn al-Jamuh's influence extended beyond his own tribe, as he worked to unite various factions within the Islamic community.

As a leader, Amr ibn al-Jamuh was instrumental in the Battle of Uhud, where he fought alongside Muhammad and other prominent Islamic figures. The battle, which took place in 625 CE, was a significant turning point in the early history of Islam, as it marked a shift from the initial phase of Islamic expansion to the later phase of consolidation and conflict.

In the aftermath of the Battle of Uhud, Amr ibn al-Jamuh continued to play a crucial role in the early Islamic state. He was appointed as the governor of Medina, a position that allowed him to exercise significant authority over the city and its inhabitants.

Despite his importance in the early days of Islam, Amr ibn al-Jamuh's legacy is not as widely known as that of other Islamic figures. However, his contributions to the development of the Islamic community and the spread of Islam throughout the Arabian Peninsula cannot be overstated.

Amr ibn al-Jamuh's significance extends beyond his own time and place, as his legacy continues to influence Islamic thought and practice to this day. His leadership and vision played a key role in shaping the early Islamic state, and his influence can still be felt in the modern world.

In recent years, Amr ibn al-Jamuh has gained increasing recognition as a key figure in Islamic history. His contributions to the development of the Islamic community have been the subject of extensive study and debate, and his legacy continues to inspire scholars and historians around the world.
